articles.title_orig: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
articles.title_zh: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
articles.content_orig:
In a resounding rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party, Democrats will control both the House and Senate for the last two years of Trump’s presidency, cementing one of the strongest midterm showings for either party in decades. The Associated Press called the upper chamber for Democrats late on Tuesday, after the party’s candidates secured victories in battleground races across the map. The outlet later called control of the lower chamber in the early hours of Wednesday morning as Democrats picked up more than two dozen seats.
The milestone potentially sets up a new political dynamic in Washington. A President has not had to deal with a Congress completely controlled by the opposition party since the last two years of Barack Obama’s presidency. Congress now stands to be a true counterweight to the White House and its agenda.
Democrats needed to net four seats to claim the Senate majority—a tough task given the map this cycle clearly favored Republicans. But with wins in Texas , Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, and Maine, Democrats achieved what most handicappers had treated as a long shot until just weeks before Election Day. Democrats in multiple toss-up Senate races managed to effectively harness a national mood against Trump, the economy and the Iran War to win in places initially deemed out of reach for the party. Outstanding Senate races in states like Michigan could potentially pad Democrats’ majority.
Read more : How Trump’s Approval Compares to Other Presidents Just Before the Midterms
The new Senate is likely to be led by Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, who will regain his title of Senate Majority Leader from Republican Senator John Thune of South Dakota. While some Democrats have criticized Schumer’s leadership as minority leader over the past two years, it’s not clear if any Senators are prepared to challenge his leadership before the next Congress convenes in January.
The size of a possible Democratic majority in the House is still unclear as votes in many states were still being tallied, but signs of a significant Trump-centered backlash were popping up all over the country Tuesday night, potentially setting up the party to come away with a double-digit majority. Strategists with both parties had predicted for months that Republicans were unlikely to hold onto the House, where they could only afford to lose three seats.
House Democrats have vowed to use a House majority to aggressively investigate Trump, his Administration, and his allies, as well as push policy proposals they campaigned on, including ending the Iran War, undoing Trump’s tariffs and lowering the cost of living.
Likely Democratic control of the House would also mean the end of Mike Johnson’s speakership, with Democrats likely set to rally behind their leader in the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, to replace him. Jeffries would be the first Black speaker in U.S. history. Read more: 10 Candidates Who Could Make History in the Midterms
Polls had been consistently pointing for months to the House flipping to Democrats. For well over a year, nearly every poll from a reputable pollster asking voters which party’s candidate they intended to support showed Democrats with a clear advantage. But Republicans managed to hold their own or do better in fundraising, especially in pivotal battlegrounds for control of the Senate. And some Democrats as recently as this past weekend were worried that they may somehow still come up short.
Republicans spent much of the year trying to make the best of a bad environment. They constantly claimed the polls were all off, that Trump could still turn out his coalition that remade the modern GOP, and that Democrats’ overconfidence could depress their own turnout.
As Election Day neared, Republicans moved into triage mode. While they initially had planned to go on the offense against incumbent Democrats, those ambitions quickly evaporated as they shifted funding away from flipping Democratic seats and toward shoring up Republicans in a wider array of districts.
By late Tuesday, as exit polls started to paint a picture of the national mood, there were signs that many polls had likely under-estimated Democrats’ strength heading into Election Day.
The new Democratic caucus in both chambers are poised to include many new faces, from those who ran as moderates to self-avowed democratic socialists who ran as much against centrist leaders like Jeffries than Trump. Now starts the messy business of this new majority figuring out what they plan to do with their power. Trump will certainly be watching closely.

articles.title_orig: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.title_zh: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
articles.content_orig:
The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.
The company’s cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it’s probably “enough” for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button.
With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone , you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.
On the software front, the device will offer a choice. You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose. It also supports OdysseyOS , a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser).
Some minor details are still up in the air. The designers aren’t yet sure about waterproofing and durability ratings, and the battery capacity could change. But they hope that spec will go up, not down, if it changes at all. Carrier support is also unclear right now. It will be an unlocked 5G phone, and the company is aiming for “broad global support.” But if you’re on a restrictive carrier like Verizon, you may be out of luck.
The other wrinkle is the timeline. The Enough Phone goes live on Kickstarter today , with shipping currently slated for May 2027. The phone might seem like enough today, but will you feel the same in six months? Plenty of Kickstarter projects have failed to deliver on time (or at all). The Enough Phone team points out that this isn’t its first smartphone effort, though. The team says it has designed and shipped hardware for other companies you’ve heard of, working as an original design manufacturer (ODM).
If you’ve been posting comments about how much you want a smaller phone, now’s your chance to do something about it. The Enough Phone starts at $399 for early backers. It will go up to $449 and then $499 later. The final MSRP will be $599. That’s not bad for a niche piece of hardware, given the rapid increase in component costs.
You will have to take a little leap of faith to get on board with the Enough Phone. The company says it plans to support the device with updates through 2032, which is almost flagship territory. But when a company like Samsung or Google makes that commitment, it’s essentially a guarantee. This is the first phone this group has made under its own brand, and there’s no telling how that will work out.

articles.title_zh: ‘Enough Phone’ is an Android phone roughly the size of iPhone 13 Mini, launching in 2027
articles.content_orig:
Everyone says they want small Android phones back, and 2027 might be your chance to actually buy one. The “Enough Phone” has a mere 5.3-inch display, decent specs, and a price of $599 and less.
Launching in May 2027, the “Enough Phone” is a 5.3-inch Android phone that simply does want to be “enough.”
The company says the 5.3-inch LCD display comes in at 1520×720 and that the phone will be powered by a MediaTek Dimensity 7500 chipset, 8GB of RAM, and offers 128GB of storage. It’ll come with either “stock Android” or OdysseyOS, an Android skin used by SLEKE and designed to be minimal and act like a modern dumbphone. SLEKE currently sells repurposed Pixel phones running this software.
Android 17 will run out of the box with updates through 2032.
“Enough Phone” measures in at 132.8 x 63.8 x 12mm and will have a battery between 3,500 and 4,000 mAh which will be user-replaceable. While it’s thicker, the physical size is roughly the same as iPhone 13 Mini.
Rounding out the package would be a fingerprint sensor in the power button, a single 50MP (Sony IMX766) camera on the back, and a 32MP selfie camera up front.
The company says that these specs are “mostly final” and that pricing is planned for $599.
“Enough Phone” is funding on Kickstarter with $399, $449, and $499 early bird reservation tiers ahead of the May 2027 shipping estimate.

articles.title_orig: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.title_zh: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.content_orig:
Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory , and particularly their coming control of the US Senate, strengthen the Federal Reserve against President Trump’s efforts to meddle with it, with the Senate’s control over appointments a major guardrail against Trump landing any more allies at the central bank.
It could also mean new headaches for Chairman Kevin Warsh, with key oversight committees now in the hands of Democrats, and in the case of the Senate Banking Committee, with Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, of Massachusetts, a harsh Warsh critic , likely replacing Trump ally and Warsh supporter Tim Scott of South Carolina as the panel’s chair.
Warsh “got no support for his chairmanship from Democrats … Hostile questioning could put Warsh’s rhetoric to the test,” as he pursues a quieter and less publicly transparent form of central banking, economists from Monetary Policy Analytics, the firm of former Fed Governor Larry Meyer, wrote about the fallout of a Democratic Senate win.
Democrats, having campaigned heavily on cost-of-living issues, have incentive to push Warsh on the central bank’s inflation mandate , while the panel will have broad room to investigate issues they regard as important — such as, in Warren’s case, Warsh’s opaque disposition of hundreds of millions of dollars in assets as he ascended to the Fed’s top job.
For Trump, the new dynamics on Capitol Hill directly stymie his effort to put more allies on the Fed’s seven-member board, three of whom were appointed by former President Joe Biden. Former Chair Jerome Powell, appointed to consecutive terms by Trump and Biden but now at odds with the president, remains on the board as well.
The president has called the configuration “hostile” and “partisan,” and argued the Fed needs to drastically cut interest rates that policymakers — including Warsh — have instead been raising to control high inflation.
Trump’s effort to fire Governor Lisa Cook remains ongoing, with a White House administrative procedure expected in coming weeks to set the stage for a Trump announcement that he has “cause” to fire her over errors on mortgage applications that predate her appointment to the Fed.
A court challenge is likely to follow. The Supreme Court has ruled against Trump once already on the effort to oust Cook, and there’s next to no prospect he would get a chosen replacement confirmed by a Democrat-led Senate if he were ultimately successful in removing her.
Even a Republican-controlled body rejected what were seen as extreme Fed appointments during Trump’s first term, and earlier this year Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who decided not to run for reelection in North Carolina after Trump threatened him in a race won by Democrat Roy Cooper on Tuesday, held up Warsh’s nomination until the administration abandoned a criminal investigation of Powell .
A Senate under Democratic control “would change the confirmation environment for future Trump nominees…and could provide the Fed with a different degree of political support,” Mark Spindel, a partner at Pilot Wave Holdings and author of a book about Fed politics, wrote in an analysis of the election’s implications.
Fed independence “has always depended in part on Congress, and institutional support from the Senate can affect how much room policymakers have to make decisions based on inflation and employment rather than political pressures.”
Democratic control of the Senate committee as well as the House Financial Services Committee could also entangle the bank and regulatory reforms pushed by the administration and by current Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman, with the Fed drafting rules over things like the Genius Act regulating stablecoins, and Bowman recently rolling out a consolidation of the Fed’s bank supervision system.

articles.title_orig: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.title_zh: CVS to Split Off Pharmacy Business, Ending the Healthcare Conglomerate Era
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate breakups in history, the company announced Wednesday.
The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS' roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs.
The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release . Shares of CVS fell more than 12% on Wednesday.
It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS' aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shake-ups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
But Joyner told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " on Wednesday that the decision to split is "out of a position of strength," pointing to recovery in Aetna's Medicare business and solid performance in the retail pharmacy.
"So it's all about the strength of the business that affords us the opportunity to make what we think are the right strategic decisions for the future of this company," he later added.
CVS shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion.
The two new companies would both be publicly traded.
The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said.
Existing CVS shareholders will own stock in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans.
The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and the healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion.
CVS on Wednesday also posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that topped Wall Street expectations. Total sales climbed to $108.40 billion, from $102.87 billion in the prior-year period.
Sales were boosted by year-over-year growth in the company's healthcare benefits and health services segments. Meanwhile, revenue in its pharmacy services business slid from the previous year.
On Wednesday, CVS said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business.
CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits.
It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units.
But Joyner told CNBC that the company was "in a turnaround" at that time without the flexibility, cash position or business performance to execute a split.
In an interview, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split shows "the stability of the pharmacy," which has won market share from competitors and is seeing gross margins stabilize thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year that the company bills as more transparent.
"This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome," he told CNBC on Wednesday.
One potential concern for investors is whether the retail pharmacy will lose its competitive advantage of being directly linked with a PBM, which negotiates drug prices and manages prescription drug benefits on behalf of insurers and employers.
But Joyner told analysts Wednesday that the synergy between the two businesses "are going to be preserved in commercial agreements between the two organizations," adding that "we don't need the integration of an operating structure."
Cherny said the rationale for the split could also extend to the state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration.
The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban co-ownership of PBMs and pharmacies. Those have been challenged in court by CVS and other companies.
PBMs have been criticized for opaque pricing practices, their growing market power and potential conflicts of interest when they are owned by companies that also operate insurers and pharmacies.

articles.title_orig: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.title_zh: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.content_orig:
China, Canada, India and South Africa could gain fresh leverage in trade negotiations with Washington after Democrats seized control of both chambers of the US Congress, weakening President Donald Trump's political position amid growing discontent over the Iran war, rising consumer prices and his controversial trade tariffs.
The November 3 midterm elections saw Republicans lose their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, with Democrats securing victories in Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.
Republicans suffered the setback amid rising living costs, Trump's tariffs and the eight-month Iran war, which disrupted energy supplies and pushed Brent crude to $138.21 per barrel in April, its highest level since 2008, fuelling US inflation.
From what Business Insider Africa has gathered, the results could encourage America's trade rivals and dissatisfied partners to resist Washington's demands, delay investments and seek better trade deals as Trump will now have to answer to a Democrat-controlled Congress.
DON'T MISS: Despite warnings from China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Israel presses ahead with embassy plans in breakaway African territory near Red Sea
China is among the countries that could use Trump's weakened political position to push for more favourable trade terms, particularly as Beijing seeks to recover exports lost to American tariffs.
The impact of those restrictions is reflected in US trade figures, which show that America's goods trade deficit with China narrowed from $295.5 billion in 2024 to $202.1 billion in 2025.
With a temporary trade truce approaching expiration in January 2027, Beijing could seek lower tariffs and fewer technology restrictions, calculating that Trump faces greater political resistance to another trade war.
Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia, believes China could take advantage of the changing political balance in Washington.
"Xi Jinping will recognize that Trump's authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that," Eslake told Reuters.
Although Beijing has not publicly indicated plans to exploit Trump's political setback, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the elections as an internal US matter, saying the country would continue managing differences and expanding cooperation with Washington.
DON'T MISS: Two Chinese mining firms pull out of Kenya’s rare earth and niobium extraction race as three American companies stand their ground among five remaining bidders
Canada could also find greater support in Washington after months of difficult trade negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump's administration over tariffs and market access.
Talks stalled in August after Ottawa rejected American demands, while tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium and other products continued to strain relations between the neighbouring economies.
In an October 30 interview with POLITICO, Carney indicated that Canada would rather wait for another American president than accept an unfavourable agreement.
Asked whether Canada could hold out until Trump's successor took office, he replied: "Well, if that's what it takes, yeah."
His position could receive support from Democrats, particularly Senator Ron Wyden, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, who has called for removing tariffs on Canadian goods because of their impact on businesses and consumers.
DON'T MISS: European nation stops foreign workers and students from South Africa, Ghana, India and other countries from applying for residence permits inside the country
India could gain negotiating flexibility as New Delhi seeks better trade terms while American consumers face higher prices on imported goods.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian products in 2025 amid trade disputes and disagreements over India's purchases of Russian oil. The restrictions affected textiles, jewellery and footwear, increasing costs for American importers.
The countries agreed in February 2026 to a framework reducing tariffs on most Indian goods to 18%, but negotiations remain unfinished.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the agreement had reached the final drafting stage, although New Delhi would proceed only if it secured an advantage over competing exporters.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also acknowledged in October that further concessions would be "very, very difficult" for both sides.
The Democratic victory could encourage India to resist additional demands as Trump faces greater scrutiny of his trade policies from the Democrat-controlled Congress.
South Africa faces a trade setback after Washington announced on November 2 that it would remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on January 1, 2027, following months of diplomatic tensions over Pretoria's domestic and foreign policies.
The decision threatens preferential access for South African exports, including vehicles, citrus fruits and wine, adding to existing trade pressures after the country's agricultural exports to the US fell by 28% in the second quarter of 2026.
President Cyril Ramaphosa previously urged South Africans to prepare for possible exclusion, saying: "We should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."
However, in a sharp reversal of his earlier cautious stance, Ramaphosa welcomed the Democratic victory on November 4, saying: "We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken."
He added that the results could introduce "a new era in world relations", raising hopes of improved ties with Washington.
"We're hoping that, on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds, where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," Ramaphosa said.

articles.title_orig: Jokes fly as Trump’s DJT stock plummets to Happy Meal prices
articles.title_zh: Jokes fly as Trump’s DJT stock plummets to Happy Meal prices
articles.content_orig:
On Wednesday, following the GOP’s historic midterm bloodbath , President Donald Trump received another humiliation when the price of his signature DJT stock plunged to its lowest point ever. While investors were once paying $175 per share, it’s worth just over $5 as of this writing, or as the internet noted , “about as much as a Happy Meal.”
DJT is the stock ticker for Trump Media & Technology Group Corp. (TMTG), the parent company for Trump’s Truth Social social media platform. Launched in 2021, early investors paid as much as $175 per share, which plunged to about $13 per share within two years. After the company went public in 2024 amidst Trump’s presidential campaign, its value briefly jumped to $61.96 but has been falling off ever since, and has been in freefall since October. Then on Election Day, as it became clear that the Republicans had been decimated by the midterms, its price went over a cliff, plummeting from just under $6 to a record low of $5.05. The internet noticed and offered its thoughts on the matter.
“Trump Media stock is down,” Washington Post contributor Drew Harwell pointed out . “A share costs about as much as a Happy Meal. At its peak, investors paid $175 a share.” But as writer Amanda Knox noted , “With a Happy Meal, you get a toy that you can keep.”
“Do not buy the dip,” warned New Yorker staff writer Philip Gourevitch. “If you're baffled by Trump voters, consider Trump investors,” mused another comment.
“Chugging this stuff until my torso kerplodes,” admitted one reshare of the disastrous stock chart. And All In producer Adam Weinstein needed no words to express his sentiments, adding only a clip from Mad Men in which character Don Draper achieves a moment of zen.
This isn’t the first time Trump’s company has been hit by bad financial news. In 2025, Truth Social reported net losses of $712 million. At the same time, data suggests that its traffic has fallen by 30 percent year over year, while its users dropped from a peak of roughly 420,000 in June 2025 to about 260,000 in September 2026. In 2023, it was also reported that TMTG was under investigation for laundering money for Russian oligarchs. While TMTG sued the Guardian and Variety for reporting on the story, the suit was dismissed. According to the Washington Post, a federal probe found that one of the company’s wealthy investors was linked to efforts to move assets from Russia, Ukraine, and China to the Caribbean. Over the past two years, the company has been increasingly involved with various cryptocurrency ventures, and the Trump family ’s crypto schemes have reportedly raked in roughly $2.3 billion since he reentered the White House.

articles.title_orig: Unofficial AUKUS inquiry recommends tearing up the 'worst' defense decision the country has ever made
articles.title_zh: Unofficial AUKUS inquiry recommends tearing up the 'worst' defense decision the country has ever made
articles.content_orig:
Australia should end the Aukus submarine plan and pursue a properly tested strategy to replace the Collins class fleet
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
I n 1998 I was appointed chief of the Australian defence force. I spent much of my career handling classified information and I understand why some things must stay secret: operational plans, intelligence sources, the capabilities on which lives depend.
But there is a difference between protecting secrets and withholding reasons. On Aukus , Australians have been denied the reasons.
That is the significant lesson I take from serving as a commissioner on the Aukus public inquiry. The government and the opposition declined written invitations to give evidence. No one serving in the Australian Defence Organisation appeared. This means the case for the most expensive defence project in our history – likely to be more than $368bn by the mid-2050s – was never put to us.
Instead, we heard from other Australians – young people, their mums and dads, and First Nations Australians – who cannot get straight answers about Aukus and its implications for them. They want to know about the nuclear issues – the waste from the submarine program and the rotation of American and British nuclear-powered submarines through Western Australia, and they want to know about the costs and why Australia is actively supporting submarine building in the US and UK through unconditional financial support.
The government may say it has not been silent. The Australian Submarine Agency has produced fact sheets, a public report and corporate plans. They assert that “only nuclear-powered submarines, acquired through the Aukus partnership, will meet Australia’s defence requirements in the decades ahead”, and that conventional submarines will be “increasingly less able to meet Australia’s needs”. They promise a “strategy of denial” and “impactful projection”. But they do not show the working: which missions, compared with what alternatives, at what cost and with what risk. An assertion is not an explanation.
Let’s start with the simplest question: what are these submarines for?
Nuclear-powered submarines are formidable machines. Their distinctive advantage is speed and endurance underwater, sustainable over long distances, but they are not much good in shallow water. Their characteristics matter most for two missions: hunting other nuclear-powered submarines, including those capable of launching nuclear weapons, and keeping pace underwater with American aircraft carrier battle groups. Conventional submarines can perform most of the other tasks Australia needs.
Impactful projection where, and against whom? If the real purpose is to hunt Chinese submarines near China’s home ports, or to escort American carriers, the government should say so – and explain why these missions serve Australia.
Alone it would be madness for us to take on China. The only plausible way we would be fighting near China’s coast is in a war begun by the United States. Building our future defence force around that possibility is a profound choice, and Australians deserve to have it put to them honestly.
Instead, it looks like this acquisition has become the strategy. We have a recent national defence strategy but there is no national security strategy to show what we are protecting, from what, and how diplomacy, the economy, climate resilience and defence fit together. The United States and the United Kingdom, our partners in Aukus, have published theirs. We should publish ours.
Meanwhile, commitments are being locked in.
From 2027, HMAS Stirling, the navy base near Perth, will host a rotating force of up to four American nuclear-powered submarines and one British. These will not be occasional visits as has been the practice till now. The government has committed up to $8bn to expand the base. Housing is being arranged for American personnel and their families – in a region where people told our inquiry about homelessness on their own doorstep.
after newsletter promotion
Australia has agreed by treaty to take responsibility for disposing of the spent fuel – highly enriched uranium – from its own submarines. The submarine agency’s own corporate plan names its failure to build disposal capability as a key risk, yet it sets no target, timeline or measure for dealing with the waste. Nuclear waste disposal will not be a new conversation for our community but it will be weapons-grade waste – and that is new!
The government says the foreign submarines will be conventionally armed for now – but what about into the future? The US is developing a nuclear-armed cruise missile for its Virginia-class boats. In supporting the Treaty of Rarotonga what conditions will Australia set, and how will they be verified? Could Stirling support nuclear strike operations even if no weapon is stored ashore? Will Stirling become a target for nuclear strike? If so, how will it be protected?
Money already committed is not a reason to commit more. Nor is urgency an excuse to skip strategy.
We have been here before. As a young naval officer, I worked with my bosses on the program to replace the aircraft carrier HMAS Melbourne. The program had been keenly debated for years under the Fraser governments before the Hawke government was elected in 1983. Within two weeks of taking office, it scrapped the carrier program. It then reviewed Australia’s strategic position through a new lens and built a new defence force around contemporary and prospective strategic needs. The Dibb review of 1986 and the 1987 defence white paper are examples of the kind of work we need to do now. It is urgent.
Our report recommends ending the Aukus submarine plan. That is not an argument against submarines. Australia needs a credible submarine capability under full Australian command and control, and a properly tested plan to replace the Collins class – a submarine chosen to suit our missions, not missions chosen to suit the submarine.
Above all, we must safeguard our capacity to decide for ourselves. Sovereignty is not ownership of a submarine or flying a flag over a base. It is the ability of an Australian government to decide what to do in Australia’s interests, including when our allies would prefer otherwise. The test is not whether we can say yes – that may look easy, but it will be hard. It is whether we can say no – and that is likely to be the toughest decision an Australia government has to make.

articles.title_orig: Dozens dead and missing after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre, officials say
articles.title_zh: Dozens dead and missing after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid centre, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of people were killed when Russia dropped at least nine bombs on a school building in southeastern Ukraine where they had taken shelter, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday, describing it as “one of the deadliest attacks of this war.”
At least 40 people have been confirmed dead and more than 30 are still unaccounted for after the attack on the building in Komyshuvakha in the Zaporizhzhia region, which local governor Mykhailo Semikin said was being used as a shelter and a humanitarian aid distribution center.
The attack on Monday caused such large scale damage that recovery efforts are still underway two days later.
Semikin said the victims were in a newly-built, EU-funded reinforced basement designed to withstand most strikes, but the massive force of the bombs caused the concrete structure to collapse and a fire broke out.
The scale of the damage is complicating the recovery works. Local authorities said that only some of the bodies recovered from the rubble as of Wednesday midday had been identified and that further identification will likely require DNA testing.
The shelter was built last year in an effort to keep classes going during wartime, but many civilians have since left as the fighting got closer to the village, and it is not currently used as a school. Instead, local authorities are using it as an administrative center and humanitarian hub.
Masha’s husband was fighting on the front line. But she was the one killed by a Russian drone
The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine highlighted that the attack took place just as civilians from the area had gathered to receive humanitarian aid.
“The timing and location of the humanitarian distribution was well publicized,” said Danielle Bell, the head of the mission.
“Either the Russian armed forces knew that there was a humanitarian distribution taking place, or they failed to take the most basic steps to find out what was happening in this village they were planning to attack. In either case, this attack seems to have violated the most fundamental principles of international humanitarian law.”
Zelensky said the attack came just before Russia launched another massive barrage of hundreds of drones and dozens of powerful cruise and ballistic missiles targeting Ukraine’s energy infrastructure – despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated calls for energy ceasefire .
Ukraine’s Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said three drones were directed at a substation that is crucial for the operation of the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant. He posted to Telegram saying actions like that threaten the nuclear safety of all of Europe, and that Ukraine has informed the UN nuclear watchdog, the IAEA.
“It is very telling that all of this is happening on the day of the US congressional elections. The Russians believe that America will not notice this signal from them. But such terror must be noticed and stopped,” Zelensky said on Tuesday morning.
“Ukraine must be helped to defend its skies, otherwise Russia will never stop its missile strikes. It is essential to help build peace honestly and reliably, and America can do that,” Zelensky added.
The latest attacks by Russia come amid a renewed push for negotiations by the Trump administration. US envoy Steve Witkoff recently held a meeting with Zelensky in Norway before flying to St. Petersburg to meet with the Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Separately, first lady Melania Trump helped to secure a ceasefire in the occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which enabled the evacuation of hundreds of civilians over the weekend. Trump’s office announced on Tuesday that the first lady would bring together representatives from Russia and Ukraine at the White House on Thursday, calling it “an extraordinary moment in American history.”
A Russian bomb attack killed at least 33 people in a Ukrainian village close to the frontline in the Zaporizhzhia region yesterday. CNN’s Clare Sebastian reports.
The strike on Monday is among the deadliest since the start of the war, but the past few months have been exceptionally bloody for Ukrainian civilians.
Russia ramped up its aerial attacks on towns and cities across the country over the summer, striking at all times of the day.
At least 33 people were killed last month when Russia hit two civilian buses in Kramatorsk in the Donetsk region. In August, 38 people were killed when a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot near the capital triggered a large fire and multiple explosions that lasted hours in a residential area near Kyiv. And a mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage.
The assault against Komyshuvakha on Monday followed a familiar scenario in which Russian forces launch the first wave of strikes, wait for emergency services to arrive and then strike again.
At least two first responders, named locally as Denys Konovalenko and Oleksiy Sushchevsky, both 44, were killed after rushing to the scene of the first strike.
The Ukrainian Police said at least four of its officers have also been killed in the attack. They were named as Mykhailo Buzhenko and Mykola Balanda, both of who had more than two decades of police service under their belts, and Mykhailo Romanov and Dmytro Besedin, both of whom have been community police officers for more than a decade.
“(They) were helping local residents take shelter in an underground school. A treacherous follow-up strike trapped everyone who was trying to escape,” the police said in a statement.
Semikin told Ukraine’s national TV broadcast on Tuesday that Russia used KAB-500 and FAB-3000 bombs in the attack.
“To put this into perspective, this is a three-ton aerial bomb containing nearly 1.5 tons of explosive material; such weapons are primarily designed to destroy heavy concrete fortifications and bunkers,” he said.
CNN’s Kit Maher, Victoria Butenko and Clare Sebastian contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: PS5 Exclusive God of War Laufey Has Officially Been Delayed by Three Months
articles.title_zh: PS5 Exclusive God of War Laufey Has Officially Been Delayed by Three Months
articles.content_orig:
Developer Santa Monica Studio has just announced its upcoming game, God of War Laufey , has been delayed.
Originally planned for release on 16th February 2027, the PS5 exclusive action game will now launch just over three months later on 20th May.
The news comes via a statement published to social media:
"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," the statement says. "We don't take for granted the trust placed in our studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans."
Santa Monica Studio says it'll "make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential."
God of War Laufey is the next entry in Sony's popular action series, chronicling the journey of Kratos' late wife, Faye, as she navigates the afterlife.
As mentioned in the above statement, the game was officially announced in June of this year, and even then it appeared to be close to release. At the time, some thought Sony was pushing Laufey harder than the imminent Marvel's Wolverine .
Still, the game will launch within a year of its announcement, which is pretty good going.

articles.title_orig: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
articles.title_zh: AI data-center stocks slide, renewables rally after Democratic US midterm sweep
articles.content_orig:
Democrats scored sweeping victories in the U.S. midterm elections on Wednesday, flipping key Republican-held seats in Congress and securing historic wins in traditionally conservative states, as voters delivered a setback to President Donald Trump.
The party was projected to gain control of both chambers of Congress, with victories across several battleground states threatening to constrain Trump's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his presidency.
Here are some of the scenes from polling stations, campaign headquarters and election-night celebrations across the United States.
Among the biggest surprises was Texas, where Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton to become the state's first Democratic U.S. senator since 1988.
Fellow Democrat Gina Hinojosa also unseated Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, becoming the state's first Latina governor and ending more than three decades of Republican control of the office.
In North Carolina, former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper flipped a Republican-held Senate seat after defeating Trump-backed Michael Whatley. Cooper will succeed retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis, who announced his departure after clashing with Trump over his tax and spending legislation.
In Georgia, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff secured reelection against Trump-backed Republican Mike Collins, while former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor's race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a U.S. state.
Meanwhile, in Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown staged a political comeback, defeating Republican incumbent Jon Husted in a closely watched Senate race.
The elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's second term, with concerns over the cost of living, inflation and the war in Iran weighing on voter sentiment.
—CNBC's Danielle DeVries contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Fire Rages for Second Day at Russia’s Key Oil Hub After Ukrainian Strike
articles.title_zh: Fire Rages for Second Day at Russia’s Key Oil Hub After Ukrainian Strike
articles.content_orig:
In brief: A massive fire continued for a second day at Russia’s Samara oil hub following a Ukrainian drone strike on Monday, Nov. 2. Operated by state-owned Transneft, the facility is one of Europe’s largest oil storage complexes, with 71 tanks holding more than 1.6 million cubic meters of crude. It serves as a critical transportation and distribution center where four major pipelines converge, connecting several Russian oil-producing regions to refineries and export routes.
A fire continued for a second day at one of Russia’s largest oil transportation hubs in the Samara region following a Ukrainian drone strike on Monday, Nov. 2, with footage showing a massive plume of smoke rising above the facility’s storage tanks.
The attack targeted the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPDS), a major facility operated by Russia’s state-owned pipeline company Transneft, located near the settlement of Prosvet, approximately 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the regional capital.
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official .
The station is one of the largest oil storage facilities in Europe, with 71 tanks holding more than 1.6 million cubic meters (56.5 million cubic feet) of crude oil. Spanning more than 216 hectares (534 acres), it serves as a critical junction in Russia’s oil transportation network, where four major pipelines converge.
Footage published by the Russian investigative outlet Astra and Ukrainian monitoring channels showed thick black smoke rising from the direction of the facility. Astra cited eyewitness accounts and footage from local residents.
Samara Region Governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev acknowledged a Ukrainian drone attack on the region but did not identify the facility as a target or report damage. He said air defense systems and mobile fire groups were operating.
The Samara LPDS is more than a storage depot. It is a major transportation and distribution center connecting oil-producing regions in Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg region, and Kazakhstan to Russia’s wider pipeline network.
Four major trunk pipelines converge at the facility: Almetyevsk-Kuibyshev, Kaltasy-Kuibyshev, Nizhnevartovsk-Kurgan–Kuibyshev, and Guryev-Kuibyshev.
The station receives, stores, and redistributes crude oil, routing supplies toward Russian refineries and export infrastructure, including the Druzhba pipeline.
It also plays a role in preparing Russia’s Urals export blend, the country’s main crude oil export grade. Oil from different producing regions is mixed to achieve the required specifications before being transported to export markets.
According to Ukraine’s General Staff , Urals accounts for as much as half of Russia’s oil exports, making facilities involved in its production and transportation strategically important to Moscow’s energy revenues.
The hub’s importance extends beyond Russia. It also handles Kazakh crude transported through the Atyrau-Samara pipeline, one of Kazakhstan’s routes for exporting oil through Russian territory.
Kazakhstan temporarily suspended oil transportation through the pipeline following Monday’s attack. Its energy ministry said pumping resumed on Tuesday after a technical inspection, with the route returning to normal operations.
The Monday strike was not the first time the Samara LPDS had been targeted. Kyiv Post previously reported several attacks on the facility in October, including strikes on Oct. 2, 7, 10, and 11.
The Oct. 7 attack caused particularly significant damage. Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed that an earlier strike on Oct. 2 had damaged 11 storage tanks with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters each and three tanks holding 50,000 cubic meters (1.7 million cubic feet) each.
Following the Oct. 7 attack, the destruction of four additional 50,000-cubic-meter storage tanks was confirmed , with satellite imagery showing the extent of the damage.
The latest attack also came amid a renewed wave of Ukrainian strikes against Russia’s refining industry.
On Oct. 30, drones struck Rosneft’s Novokuibyshevsk refinery in the Samara Oblast. The following day, Bashneft’s Novoil refinery in Ufa, in Russia’s Republic of Bashkortostan, was hit.
On Sunday, the Lukoil-Nizhegorodnefteorgsintez ( NORSI ) refinery in the Nizhny Novgorod Oblast was targeted, while a fire broke out at the Novo-Yaroslavl refinery ( Slavneft-YANOS ) following a reported drone attack.
Ukraine had temporarily paused attacks on Russian refineries following US President Donald Trump’s request to President Volodymyr Zelensky not to target Russian fuel production.
However, attacks on other elements of Russia’s oil infrastructure, including transportation and storage facilities, have continued.
Kyiv Post is Ukraine’s first and oldest English news organization, reporting since 1995. Its international reach – 90% of readers are outside of Ukraine – make it truly Ukraine’s global voice.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon
articles.title_zh: SpaceX Starship Will Need To Re-Fuel 22 Times In Space To Make It To The Moon
articles.content_orig:
As NASA plans to send astronauts back to the surface of the Moon in 2028 , there's still the small matter of figuring out how to get them there. While the Artemis II mission proved that we can send people around the Moon and bring them safely home, the space agency needs a way to take astronauts out of the Orion capsule and down to the actual ground. The original plan was for a SpaceX Starship to fulfill this duty, and that could still be the case. But delays in the development of that ambitious rocket caused NASA to re-open the contract, which allowed Blue Origin to toss its hat in the ring . Still, SpaceX insists it will fend off this challenge from a rival billionaire-owned space company and win the contract all over again. The only thing standing in its way: the minor fact that it has to refuel the Starship in-orbit, something never done before and that SpaceX hasn't even attempted yet. Oh, and it has to do it many, many times. How many? Great question.
The NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel recently announced that, by their calculations, a Starship would require fully 22 in-orbit refuelings to get that one single rocket to the Moon's surface, per Ars Technica . Again, the total number of times that any rocket has ever done this is zero. Specifically, the plan from SpaceX is to launch one Starship into orbit to act as a fuel depot; then launch many other Starships to load up that first one with fuel; then launch a final Starship to take on that fuel from the depot and head out to the Moon.
If 22 sounds like an insane number to you, you're not alone: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said on the social media platform X, which SpaceX owns, "Actual number will be more like 6 to 8." That makes for quite a broad range of estimates. The reason this is so fuzzy is because the fuel we're talking about here isn't gasoline, but rather a mixture of liquid oxygen and methane . This actually boils off in the vacuum of space, so how much fuel can be transferred depends on the efficiency of the technology involved. Technology that has never actually been tested in orbit.
Currently, SpaceX plans to perform its first test of orbital refueling in early 2027 , just a little over a year before it will theoretically do it for the Moon landing. If that doesn't work, well, SpaceX's lunar ambitions are in trouble. Even if it does go well, and there are absolutely no issues whatsoever with this unprecedented capability, there's still the small matter of actually launching all of these rockets. Right now, the still-in-development Starship only launches once every few months. Musk claims it will be launching weekly by early 2027, just months away. And then he further claims it will launch twice a week by the end of 2027. Let's just say that would be, ah, truly remarkable if it happened.
For once, let us be optimistic, and believe in words. If these words be true, and Starship truly is launching twice-weekly, then launching 22 refueling Starships (plus launching the initial "depot" Starship) would take... three months. And that is assuming no failures, either of the rockets or of the fuel transfer process. That's reduced to three weeks if you also believe Musk's figure of six launches. At least Musk has never once lied about his companies capabilities! If for some reason you don't believe in that launch cadence, then total refueling will take potentially years . Either way, that would amount to the most complicated endeavor NASA, or any space entity, has ever attempted.
By contrast, Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin has a much simpler plan to get to the Moon. It's still complicated, let's be clear, but less so than SpaceX. The company's proposal calls for a mere four launches of its New Glenn rocket, assuming it doesn't explode and destroy its entire launchpad, again . The first three would park a booster stage in orbit; the fourth would put a Blue Moon lunar lander into orbit, where it will collect all the booster stages, stack them together, and then blast off towards the Moon. That is a wild dance all its own, but it doesn't require figuring out how to transfer any fuel.
If you're wondering where the actual astronauts are, don't you worry: they're on a completely different rocket altogether. The Space Launch System (SLS) rocket carries the Orion capsule into orbit with all the astronauts on board. The capsule then continues on from Earth orbit to lunar orbit on its own, as the Artemis II mission demonstrated. Somewhere along that path — whether in high-Earth orbit, high-lunar orbit, or low-lunar orbit (this part still isn't nailed down) — the Orion capsule will have to dock with either the Starship or the Blue Moon, depending on who wins the contract. The lander will then land, the astronauts will enjoy a nice walk around another world, and then the lander will return to lunar orbit. Then it's back aboard the Orion capsule and then back to Earth.
Sounds easy! Basically, a lot has to go right for NASA to make that 2028 landing date. How it shakes out in practice depends on how well a lot of untested equipment and procedures work. Then again, if you were to go back to the 1960s, the Apollo program wasn't exactly any more precedented, or safer. In that decade, though, NASA did have a lot more testing demonstrations before going for the Moon. This time around, the agency wants to get there faster.

articles.title_orig: A Lawsuit Says the McRib Is Lacking Something You Might Expect It to Have
articles.title_zh: A Lawsuit Says the McRib Is Lacking Something You Might Expect It to Have
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's has found itself in the middle of a bizarre lawsuit alleging that its cult-favorite McRib sandwich doesn't include rib meat.
The New York Times reported this week that Judge April M. Perry ruled in United States District Court in Chicago ruled that a class-action lawsuit against the fast-food giant over could proceed.
The lawsuit claims that McDonald's is misleading consumers in its branding of the seasonal sandwich that returned to select restaurants for a limited time on Oct. 26.
McDonald's says the sandwich features "seasoned boneless pork patty" slathered in BBQ sauce and topped with slivered onions and tart dill pickles, all on a homestyle bun. It made its debut in the United States in 1981 as a limited-time item in the Kansas City area and quickly became a fan-favorite.
But the lawsuit says rib meat, an expensive prized part of a pig, isn't in the sandwich. According to the Times, the lawsuit alleges "deliberate sleight of hand," asks for monetary damages and calls on the company to "desist from further naming, marketing and advertising practices" that mislead customers.
In 2013, McDonald's acknowledged to ABC News that the meat was pork shoulder.
McDonalds said in a statement in January, when the suit was filed, that "this lawsuit distorts the facts and the claims are meritless."

"Our fan-favorite McRib sandwich is made with 100 percent pork sourced from farmers and suppliers across the U.S.," the company said, per the Times. "There are no hearts, tripe or scalded stomach used in the McRib patty as falsely alleged in this lawsuit."
Perry noted that allowing the suit to continue did not mean she agreed with everything the plaintiffs alleged.
McDonald's operates more than 40,000 restaurants in more than 100 countries worldwide.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's leader says Russian "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70 people, pleads for air defenses
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's leader says Russian "insane attack" on aid center may have killed 70 people, pleads for air defenses
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv — The death toll from a Russian missile strike on a Ukrainian aid distribution center climbed to 40, President Zelenskyy said in a Wednesday post on social media. Zelenskyy said Russia dropped nine bombs on an old school being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Ukraine's southeast Zaporizhzhia  region on Monday.
"They first struck people who had come to receive humanitarian aid, and then first responders and police officers who arrived at the scene," Zelenskyy wrote , noting that rescue efforts were still ongoing Wednesday afternoon, and "more than 30 people may still be under the rubble."
Russia's Defense Ministry said a strike in the area targeted Ukraine's military, and it claimed that as many as 25 Ukrainian service members were killed. Russia denies deliberately targeting civilians, despite strikes regularly hitting apartment buildings and other civilian infrastructure.
On Tuesday, Russia launched one of its largest attacks of the year on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, hitting facilities in 10 different regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry.
The attacks affected the Ukrainian capital's water supply, with Kyiv residents losing running water in their homes for more than 16 hours. Kyivvodokanal, the city's water utility, said water supply and sewage pumping stations in Kyiv resumed operations on Wednesday afternoon.
Russian and Ukrainian representatives will visit the White House Friday to meet with Melania Trump, after the first lady brokered a temporary ceasefire last week to allow for civilian evacuations and humanitarian aid to move into Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine, officials in both Kyiv and Moscow said.
Ukrainian Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets and Davyd Arakhamiia, the leader of Zelenskyy's parliamentary faction, will attend the meeting, according to Ukrainian newspaper Ukrinform .
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev and Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova planned to represent Russia at the meeting, but that visa complications could affect their travel.
Zelenskyy announced Wednesday that the U.S. first lady was to receive Ukraine's highest award for women, the Order of Princess Olga, 1st Class, for her role in brokering the limited ceasefire.
He also promised a Ukrainian response to the Russian attack on the Zaporizhzhia aid center, and a day after Democrats took control of both houses of the U.S. Congress, he renewed his plea for more missile interceptors and other key military support.
"Unfortunately, there has been very little reaction from the world to this insane attack. But it, like thousands upon thousands of other war crimes Russia has committed against Ukraine and Ukrainians, demands a strong response," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Evil always goes further if it is left unanswered. We count on a response – Ukraine needs air defense support right now. I am grateful to the partners who are taking such steps."

articles.title_orig: UK national tests positive for Ebola virus in DR Congo
articles.title_zh: UK national tests positive for Ebola virus in DR Congo
articles.content_orig:
A British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo will be flown back to the UK.
It is the first confirmed case of a UK national contracting Ebola during the most recent outbreak of the rare but deadly virus in DR Congo, which has so far led to more than 5,000 deaths.
It is not clear when the flight will take place.
Earlier, a UK government spokesperson said there were "well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this" and that the risk to the public remains low.
Reuters news agency reported the infected man is a healthcare worker, citing an internal document BBC News has not seen.
Imported Ebola cases are extremely rare in the UK and have resulted in no deaths.
There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK - one, in 1976, resulting from a laboratory incident, and three involving health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.
A UK government spokesperson said: "The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated.
"Further information will be shared in due course as appropriate. The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low."
There have been more than 10,000 confirmed cases since the recent outbreak in DR Congo started in May, which has grown to become the second most deadly recorded spate of infections, behind the outbreak in West Africa.
It has since become the deadliest in the country's history, with a fatality rate of 48.6% reported at the end of last month.
Ebola can result in serious illness and death. Early symptoms include vomiting and diarrhoea but it can progress to organ failure and internal bleeding.
The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The ongoing outbreak centred on DR Congo is fueled by the Bundibugyo variant of the virus.
There is no approved vaccine but the World Health Organisation said experts have recommended adding two new candidate drugs to an ongoing clinical trial.
The vaccines, one developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and another by the firm Moderna, will join the trial once they are approved by Congolese health authorities.
It will be the first time jabs specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus are tested during an outbreak.
Since the outbreak, Ebola cases have also been confirmed in Kenya, Nigeria and Uganda.
Additional reporting by Richard Kagoe

articles.title_zh: I tried Apple’s Siri Recaps. They’re surprisingly useful — and a little unsettling
articles.content_orig:
Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

On Tuesday, Apple rolled out a potentially controversial set of Audio Intelligence features into testing with the first developer beta versions of iOS 27.3 and watchOS 27.3. The betas bring four new AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
After just a day with Apple’s Siri Recaps feature on my Apple Watch, I can already see how its value may ultimately outweigh any creepiness factor that comes from the AI-powered audio recording and summarization it provides. However, I also see areas where AI-assisted note-taking can go too far, capturing things that aren’t worth remembering, and where there’s room for improvement.
The first two, sound and song detection, don’t represent potential privacy concerns; they are designed to detect either important sounds — like an alarm or doorbell — or identify a song using Shazam’s technology. The former helps deaf and hard-of-hearing users navigate the world, and the latter is something we’ve already done with our iPhone for nearly two decades now.
It’s the two other features, Live Rewind and Siri Recaps, that have raised concerns. The features record and then transcribe or summarize the conversations happening with and around the Apple Watch’s owner. Live Rewind lets you go back to see what was said in the past 15 seconds, while Siri Recaps summarize audio throughout your day, saving notes of the important things that were said.
Apple has taken care to ensure the privacy of these AI features by processing the audio and running AI models on-device, when possible, and by not identifying speakers, storing raw audio files, and redacting private information, like government ID numbers or personal account information.
Still, some are put off by the idea that we’re now normalizing the idea that technology is always listening .
I find myself sympathizing with both camps. I often lament that we’ve allowed technology to become so pervasive in our daily lives, but I still see the value in what Apple has built.
I haven’t yet had an appropriate time to test Live Rewind, nor do I think this will be a feature I use as often. I’m more likely to say “sorry, what?” or “can you repeat that?” if I missed something that was said, before turning to my Apple Watch for help.
But with Siri Recaps, I immediately saw how this could become a feature I rely on regularly to save important notes for later.
I was able to test the feature in a real-world scenario yesterday, when we were dropping off my teen’s car for repairs and picking up a rental. At both places, employees shared a lot of information about time frames, prices, and policies that were delivered verbally. The information came too fast to stop and write anything down. Yet when I returned to Siri Recaps later in the day, it had captured key details that I may need to refer back to.
For instance, it noted the deductible, the repair time frame, the amount of gas we had in the rental at the start, and other things I wanted to remember.
One complaint is that Siri Recaps had mixed this information with other topics that were later discussed in the home, like an errand we needed to run and what time babysitting was this week, something we were discussing in order to create an appointment on the family calendar with an appropriate alert time frame.
I think these items should have been saved in a separate note titled “family schedule and errands,” rather than in the same note with the car repairs, but under a separate heading.
Because I configured Siri Recaps to run at all times, it also captured non-essential things, like our “plan” to watch the midterms coverage on TV, which is not the kind of thing you’d normally jot down a note about. It also was a stark reminder that the feature was listening in on our everyday conversations. That’s something that could feel invasive in different scenarios, if the subject being discussed was more personal in nature.
This had me considering turning off the Recap feature while at home in the evening, so family dinner table chatter doesn’t become note fodder.
While I appreciated that the Recap picked up a reminder about an errand I needed to run from one of the family conversations, other tidbits it saved — like what we were watching on TV — would only be valuable if you were exporting a Siri Recap note to Apple’s Journal app, because it was something you wanted to record for personal reasons.
I’d like to see these sorts of extraneous details saved as separate notes — or at least as dedicated sections that could be exported or deleted on their own at the end of the day.
I’d also love to be able to swipe left on an individual bullet point to remove it from the Siri Recap entirely, rather than having to enter edit mode, place the cursor, and then start deleting the text I don’t need.
Another option I’d like to have would be a setting that would allow you to automatically export any saved Siri Recap (the ones you click the bookmark icon to save) to Apple’s Notes app, instead of that being an extra step.
These Recaps could go into their own folder in the Notes app for easy reference. I can understand why this option is not the default, given how many different ways people use a general-purpose app like Notes. However, it would be useful for those of us who want to keep Notes as the central starting point for all our jotted-down reminders and to-dos.
Though I wasn’t immediately warmed up to the idea that my Watch was always listening, so to speak, I see the value of this sort of automated note-taking in daily life.

articles.title_orig: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.title_zh: Business Leaders React As a 'Blunami' Sweeps America on Election Night
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 midterm elections delivered shocking wins for Democrats on Tuesday evening, reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Business leaders, tech executives, and investors are now assessing what the new political landscape could mean for their industries as Democratic candidates flipped key Senate and House seats.
This includes Texas, where James Talarico won his Senate race despite over $150 million in funding from Elon Musk for his Republican rival, Ken Paxton.
After the results, some of the tech and business leaders who sought closer ties with President Donald Trump ahead of his return to the White House could face new congressional scrutiny.
In California, the results of the nation's first-ever ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% wealth tax on residents with net worth exceeding $1 billion could have major implications for the state's elite, though as of around 7 a.m. ET, the "No" vote held a strong lead.
Here's how powerbrokers in business and tech reacted to the midterms results amid the blue wave sweeping across the country:
Reid Hoffman , the cofounder of LinkedIn and a Democratic megadonor, reacted to the party's big wins in a post on X Tuesday evening.
"Voters made clear they demand a different kind of country. Americans want an economy that can compete globally and deliver for them at home. And they made clear that they want leaders they can trust to fight for their constituents," he wrote.
"This night blew the doors off our expectations. From Texas to Ohio, Kentucky to Iowa, and South Carolina to Indiana, voters rejected the status quo. Tonight's lesson: Never discount any voter in any place," he continued.
Hoffman has been active in politics and vocal about his support for Democrats, spending tens of millions this election cycle. He also spent millions to support Kamala Harris's campaign in 2024.
Hoffman has previously said the Democratic Party had alienated Silicon Valley and was partly to blame for its shift to the right.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions to support Republicans, broke his silence late on election night with two short X posts.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said, referencing concerns that Democratic wins could mean more scrutiny on data center development.
"Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn't work this time," he joked in a quick follow-up post.
Musk, the world's richest person, spent more money than any other individual in the midterms, donating a whopping $446 million, mostly in Texas, the state he calls home along with his companies Tesla and SpaceX.
In addition to Talarico's Senate seat, the Texas governorship was also won by a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa. It was the first time in decades a Democrat won a statewide race in the Lone Star state.
Lisa Su, the CEO of chipmaker AMD, saw the election results as showing that tech companies need to do more to convince people about the benefits of AI.
"At the end of the day, what we need to do is ensure that everybody wins from AI," she said in an interview on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
"I do think this is an opportunity for us as a tech industry to realize that we need to make sure that the value proposition is clear to every local community that is going to host a data center, and I believe we can do that," she added.
Dara Khosrowshahi , the CEO of Uber, shared his thoughts on the midterms in a Wednesday morning interview with CNBC.
"I think the people of our country sent a message regarding change," he said. "I think that continuous inflation really has taken a mark on the consumer."
"I think it's up to businesses and up to our politicians and leaders in Washington to respond, and I hope that they do, because it was a very clear message that was sent out."
Khorowshahi, who is Iranian by birth, was a vocal critic of Trump during his first term, but donated $1 million to the president's inaugural fund after the 2024 election.
Keith Rabois held executive roles at PayPal, LinkedIn, and Square, before becoming managing director at Khosla Ventures. As the results came in overnight, he posted on X: "Another reason to move to Miami."
It came shortly after the Associated Press called Florida's US Senate race for the Republican incumbent, Ashley Moody, who held on despite a strong Democratic swing.
While two of the city's three main congressional districts elected Democrats in huge swings, the one that covers downtown Miami looks set to narrowly reelect the Republican incumbent, with 99% of the vote counted.
Rabois is married to Jacob Helberg, Trump's undersecretary of state for economic affairs, and their wedding ceremony was officiated by Sam Altman.
Last year, The Wall Street Journal reported the couple was selling their Miami Beach home for $65 million as Helberg relocated to Washington, DC, although Rabois planned to stay based in Miami.
Brad Gerstner , CEO of Altimeter Capital, had thoughts on how the US data center buildout would be affected by the elections.
In a guest appearance on the All-In podcast livestream Tuesday evening, Gerstner said fears that a "blue tsunami" could make it difficult to build new data centers are "overblown."
But he said that election results could slow down the development of the centers, and candidates like Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who won the Texas gubernatorial race Tuesday, could "issue a moratorium on new data centers." He said this could be "really challenging for the AI infratrade."
Gerstner also said that Republicans and the AI community have "struggled with the messaging" over AI as the affordability crisis has weighed on Americans' minds.
The investor is the architect of "Trump Accounts," the investment vehicle for children in the country that launched in July.
Dylan Patel, CEO of SemiAnalysis, hinted at what he believes a blue wave could mean for the AI buildout.
"I am now bullish space datacenters," Patel said in a post on X alongside a screenshot of results out of Texas that showed Hinojosa with an early lead over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.
Ahead of the midterms, some in tech expressed concern that Democratic wins would mean additional scrutiny on data centers, which have faced fierce opposition in communities across the US.
Dan Ives, a veteran Wall Street analyst and AI bull, said the midterms will put the brakes on the rapid construction of data centers.
In a post on X, he said the "Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years."
Ives added that while some investors will prefer a slower pace, others will view it as added risk.
"We estimate 10% of data centers will not happen now," he said.
Richard Branson, the billionaire founder of the Virgin Group, wrote in a post on LinkedIn that the results of the midterm election are not just "a decisive repudiation of Trump" but also an encouraging sign "about the limits of money in politics."
Branson wrote, "As a successful entrepreneur, I have felt embarrassed by the billions that tech entrepreneurs and hedge fund managers have spent on — mostly Republican — campaigns this election cycle, in an attempt to buy influence and control over public policy."
Branson added that voters looked past the "hateful and false messages" fueled by the billions spent on funding candidates, voting based on the issues that mattered to them.
"I hope this will prompt the next Congress to start a fresh conversation about the toxic impact of money in politics and the need for meaningful campaign finance reform," he wrote.

articles.title_zh: IDF identified Deif, other top Hamas commanders entering tunnels on eve of Oct. 7
articles.content_orig:
There were many reasons why the air force and the IDF Southern Command each failed to prevent major aspects of Hamas’s October 7, 2023 invasion, but one reason that has emerged from the IDF’s probes, and was finally belatedly approved for publication, was the potential attempt(s) to assassinate Hamas Military Chief Mohammed Deif.
It turns out that in the early morning of October 7, while IDF chief of staff Lt.-Gen. Herzi Halevi , IDF Southern Command Chief Maj. Gen. Yaron Finkleman, and others were trying to understand if Hamas was planning some kind of an attack (a small attack in between two to eight locations, not a massive penetration in 114 spots), Air Force Chief Maj. Gen. Tomer Bar spent hours probing if there was a chance to assassinate Deif.
In fact, Bar and the IDF had tracked Deif leaving his house and entering Hamas’s underground network on his way to the underground command center. The focus on assets to further such an assassination plan might have been used to better understand Hamas’s intentions.
Finkleman was also investing significant resources into understanding where Deif was located, and how he and other top Hamas officials were working to figure out whether they were planning an invasion.
All of this may sound strange knowing, after-the-fact, that Israel was facing the most dangerous invasion in 50 years.
But at the time, Bar, Finkleman, and essentially all of the other top Israeli security officials did not view a major surprise attack as even remotely likely.
In contrast, they had tried to assassinate Deif many times over a decade, twice even wounding him, but had always failed to finish him off.
Also, before October 7, many still viewed Deif as more important and dangerous than Hamas’s Gaza Chief Yahya Sinwar.
On the morning of October 7, at 7:58 a.m., it was Deif who notified all of Gaza and the world about the invasion and called on all Gazans and other members of the Iranian axis to join forces to try to overwhelm Israel.
Eventually, Sinwar was recognized as the ideological architect of a major invasion, even if Deif managed the military planning, and he became viewed as Israel’s top target.
Deif was finally killed in July 2024 and Sinwar in October 2024 after initially failing to catch or kill either of them in the invasions of northern Gaza, Khan Yunis, and Rafah.
It has also recently been approved for publication that an IDF drone observed Gazan terrorists removing coverings from rockets aimed at Israel, which could have signaled greater readiness for a wider attack.
Despite this and other signs, no top IDF officer had the full picture of what was going on, and those who did believed the worst-case scenario was a small attempt to breach into one or two villages in Israel.
