articles.title_zh: Beloved fast-food burger franchise files for bankruptcy amid plummeting revenue
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Outback Steakhouse’s largest U.S. franchisee has filed for bankruptcy , putting 61 western restaurants up for sale as the chain’s parent company seeks to take them over.
Out West Restaurant Group, also known as Cerca Trova Restaurant Group, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy Monday after years of declining sales and rising costs. Its financial troubles date back to 2018, when falling restaurant traffic began eating into revenue. The pandemic further deepened the losses, with revenue plunging 35 percent in 2020, according to court filings .
The franchisee has reached a $26.3 million agreement with Outback’s parent company, Bloomin’ Brands, to sell its restaurants and assets. The deal serves as a “stalking horse” bid, establishing a minimum starting price that other potential buyers can attempt to beat during the bankruptcy process.
Bloomin’ Brands is providing up to $5.5 million to keep the restaurants open during bankruptcy with no immediate changes expected for customers or employees.
The steakhouse chain has around 115 franchised restaurants in the U.S., along with about 544 company-owned locations. If Bloomin’ Brands completes the acquisition, it would take direct control of more than half of Outback’s remaining U.S. franchised restaurants, according to Restaurant Dive .
Bloomin’ said it was “working closely with Out West, its lenders, and other stakeholders throughout the Bankruptcy Court-supervised process as it focuses on maintaining stability in Out West’s restaurant operations, supporting Team Members and continuing to serve guests,” Restaurant Dive reports.
The company said that buying Out West’s restaurants “gives [Bloomin’] direct operational insight, allows it to invest in the units through its development initiatives, and to mitigate disruption to guests and employees.”
Out West’s restaurants are primarily located in the Southwest with locations in Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico and Colorado. The company also has significant creditors in California, according to bankruptcy filings cited by Restaurant Dive .
News of the bankruptcy filing comes as Outback revamps its menu and kitchen practices to improve food quality and win back diners.
The changes include adding a New York strip to its regular menu for the first time and introducing a thick-cut ribeye called the “Down Under Delmonico.” Outback is also updating its cut specifications, hand-trimming techniques and seasoning methods for existing favorites, including its center-cut sirloin, Rockhampton ribeye and Victoria’s barrel-cut filet mignon, the company said.
Bloomin' Brands also owns Carrabba's Italian Grill, Bonefish Grill and Fleming's Prime Steakhouse & Wine Bar.

articles.title_orig: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.title_zh: What Trump’s midterms setback could mean for Iran, Israel and Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The US midterm elections could have consequences far beyond the country’s borders. President Donald Trump has spent nearly two years overturning decades of American foreign policy, unsettling allies and adversaries alike. Now, both are watching to see how an electoral setback at home will shape his actions abroad.
For Iran, Israel and Ukraine, the stakes go well beyond who controls Congress. The result could influence whether Trump pursues a deal with Tehran or more war, how much Washington’s longstanding support for Israel erodes, and how hard he pushes Kyiv to accept terms to end Russia’s war.
Democrats will have new tools to challenge Trump. But he still has considerable freedom to act abroad, leaving world leaders with a question: Will defeat make him more willing to compromise, or more determined to get his way?
Here’s how the vote could impact Washington’s most pressing foreign policy concerns:
Iran is celebrating Trump’s midterm setback, but it is bracing for what comes next: a possible new US strike or a fresh push for a deal.
Trump admitted in a call with Fox News that the war in Iran was partly to blame for the Republicans’ losses but Vice President JD Vance was more explicit, saying in a lengthy X post Wednesday that “the reason we lost is the war.”
After eight months of striking the region’s economic lifelines to turn American voters against the war, Tehran has hailed the Republican loss as a public verdict on it. Trump acknowledged that war-driven price hikes played a role.
“If the US government betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who has led negotiations with the US, wrote on X.
Tehran is not betting on a change of course in Washington. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said anyone who believes the results will shift US policy is “deeply mistaken,” and officials say Iran’s strategy doesn’t hinge on American elections as they prepare for more war while intensifying diplomacy.
The risk of escalation is real. Reports that Trump might order new, more intense strikes are fueling anxiety across the region, and Tehran has warned that its retaliation would be much wider in scope than in earlier rounds. This week, Trump told some journalists he is considering striking Iran hard, and others that he has no immediate plans to escalate.
Top Republicans blame Iran war for midterm results
“The Iran war has become a political albatross around his neck, leaving (Trump) with a stark choice: cut a face-saving deal and declare victory, or double down militarily to reclaim the initiative,” Ali Vaez of International Crisis Group told CNN. “The danger is that a president weakened at the ballot box may seek redemption on the battlefield.”
Diplomacy offers another path. Talks that stagnated over the summer have picked up in the past week, with Tehran sending officials to Qatari mediators who are circulating proposals with Washington. Before the vote, Iran offered to open the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Trump agreed to its seven conditions.
Sanam Vakil of Chatham House said Iran’s leadership “might feel vindicated,” but that “does not necessarily solve their problems.” Trump needs a diplomatic victory yet may be reluctant to appear weak, she said, while Tehran could read his setback as a chance to demand greater concessions. She expects intensified diplomacy alongside military threats, with an interim Strait of Hormuz deal “more realistic” than a comprehensive one.
In Israel, the election day announcement that Trump would abruptly cut off US military aid to the country was the first surprise. The results, with Democrats sweeping both chambers of Congress in what has been called a “blue tsunami,” are a five-alarm fire in Israel.
Bipartisan support for Israel in the US had already been eroding, with Democrats outraged at Israel over the death toll in the Gaza war and a growing number of Republicans believing the US has given it too much support.
“The only bipartisan issue right now is criticism of Israel,” said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to the US. “It’s an organizing principle for the Democratic Party,” he told CNN. “And it’s becoming an organizing principle for much of the Republican Party.”
Oren said the end of US aid is just the beginning of a process that has only started to play out. He said it’s conceivable that the US could end intelligence sharing with Israel and the joint development of critical military systems, such as the vaunted Iron Dome aerial defense system. He also pointed to the United Nations Security Council, where Republican and Democratic presidents have protected Israel with the US veto.
“We are at the end of an era,” he said.
Trump’s Election Day bombshell on Israel points to historic shift in US politics
Yaakov Katz, a former editor-in-chief of the Jerusalem Post, warned there is more to come. “What Trump announced about the military aid yesterday is just the tip of the iceberg of what can change – arms sales could be blocked, sanctions will be proposed and joint economic programs defunded,” he said on X.
The anti-Israel sentiment only hardened during the Iran war, with segments of the US electorate viewing the joint US-Israel strikes as a war that Netanyahu sold to Trump. Even now, Netanyahu has been pushing to resume strikes on Iran, which would reignite a war that drove gas prices and the cost of living higher and contributed to Republicans’ devastating midterm performance.
Netanyahu also faces turmoil at home. In elections a week before the midterms, he lost his majority in parliament, but his main rival, former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot, does not have an outright majority and would likely need to cooperate with Arab parties, who saw record turnout.
Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats party, warned that Israel “does not have time to waste” in replacing Netanyahu and leading the country away from sanctions and isolation.
For Kyiv, the reaction came before the election. And on Wednesday there was relative silence.
For weeks, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s relationship with Trump has been in freefall. Trump has demanded Zelensky be replaced; courted energy deals to benefit Russia; and watched as Ukraine’s tech and intel dependencies on the US were inexplicably thwarted. And so Kyiv was forced to take a position early: wait, with urgency, for a post-Trump world.
And when it began to dawn on Wednesday, there was little official comment from Kyiv, Zelensky perhaps happy for the memes of him, sat with a beer and popcorn in front of the mid-term TV coverage, to do the job for him.
A deputy in his office, Sergiy Kyslytsia, pledged on Ukrainian TV that the country would continue to “develop genuine, normal and stable relations” with whoever is in office, seek Patriot interceptors, and navigate both a new Congress and the likely flurry of executive orders that may try to obviate it.
But there can be no disguising that a crestfallen Trump, and the slow clock now loudly ticking on his worldview and presidency, is in Kyiv’s favour. He had claimed a peace was easy to fashion, yet proceeded to punish Ukraine for not agreeing to the demands of its invader. He humiliated, scolded, and then occasionally made up with, Zelensky, while massaged by European allies, aghast at the breakdown in decades of security alliances.
There is still a lot that Ukraine needs Trump and the United States to do. Provide arms, money, and a wider assurance it is on their side. But Kyiv has calculated it cannot depend on Washington, after months of hostility.
There is one downside of the ticking clock however: that Russian President Vladimir Putin determines he has likely a year to pursue, at any cost, the best outcome possible in his war of choice, before the 2028 fight drags Republican policy back to the pro-Ukrainian mainstream. articles.title_orig: Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
articles.title_zh: Anker’s new window-mounted camera monitors the outside of your home from within it
articles.content_orig:
Anker’s eufy brand has launched the Window Camera E10 in the United States, a plug-in security camera that sticks to the inside of a window and looks out over a yard, driveway or entry, according to eufy in an email to iPhone in Canada on Monday. The design is aimed at people who want outdoor coverage without the usual outdoor installation headaches, and it lands as the company continues to expand a smart home lineup Canadians have already seen priced locally .
In Canada, the E10 is available now at $99.99 CAD through Anker’s Canadian online store, with shipping expected in early November. Amazon Canada and Best Buy availability is expected starting next year. US pricing starts at $79.99 . Core live view, local recording and AI detection do not require a monthly subscription, though optional cloud storage remains available if you prefer it.
Resolution reaches 2.5K (2688 × 1520), with an anti-reflection wraparound body and included anti-reflection stickers meant to cut glare from glass and indoor lights. A manual dial on the rear tilts the lens down by as much as 25 degrees so more of the frame covers packages, visitors and doorstep activity instead of empty sky. Colour night vision is built in without a spotlight, dual-band Wi-Fi on 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz supports continuous recording, and local storage uses a microSD card up to 256 GB that is sold separately.
Mounting relies on a reusable adhesive sticker for interior window glass, with a USB-C power cable about three metres long plus clips for tidy routing indoors. Human, vehicle and pet alerts run through the Anker eufy app, and the camera can work on its own or with supported eufy HomeBase units for expanded recording options.
Unlike weatherproof outdoor models such as the eufy SoloCam S340 , or the latest Ring security cameras rolling out in Canada , the E10 never leaves the warm side of the glass. That keeps siding, brick and outdoor wiring out of the job, which is the main reason the window approach can feel simpler than a classic exterior install.

ROSELAND, N.J. , Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Private-sector employment increased by 86,000 jobs in October, according to the ADP National Employment ReportÂ® produced by ADP Research in collaboration with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab ("Stanford Lab").
Base pay for private-sector workers rose 3.2% and gross pay was up 4.7% year over year, according to ADP Pay Insights.
The ADP National Employment Report is an independent measure of the labor market based on the anonymized weekly payroll data of more than 26 million private-sector employees in the United States. ADP Pay Insights uses payroll transaction data to compare the wage growth of individual workers over 12-month intervals, resulting in more than 14.7 million year-over-year pay-change observations each month.
Together, these reports use ADP's finely-grained data to provide a representative and high-frequency picture of the private-sector labor market.
"Employers of all sizes were hiring last month, and our data suggests that job-changers were lured by a combination of bonuses, overtime, and more hours in addition to higher base pay," said Dr. Nela Richardson, chief economist, ADP. "Taken together, earnings growth for these workers hit its fastest pace since March 2024."

articles.title_orig: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.title_zh: Israel's president begins consultations with parties after election deadlock
articles.content_orig:
President Isaac Herzog received the official results from the Central Election Committee on Wednesday morning
Israel's President Isaac Herzog has begun consultations with political parties on whom to task with forming a new coalition government, after he received the official results of a general election last week he said had no clear winner.
Herzog told party leaders that "not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled" if they want to avoid a new election.
Neither the bloc of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his rival Gadi Eisenkot secured a majority in parliament.
Earlier, electoral officials said there was no evidence of irregularities and that unsubstantiated claims by Netanyahu's camp of Arab-led parties "stealing" the election did not justify delaying the results' certification.
The Shin Bet security service is investigating allegations of foreign interference in the election, but the head of the Central Elections Committee stressed that they would not fundamentally change the outcome.
Israeli opposition accuses Netanyahu of trying to 'delegitimise' election
How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
Israel's election deadlock is a sign of the country's deep divisions
In the election on 27 October, Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That makes them potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
The role of Israel's president is largely ceremonial, but after an election they have the role of inviting a Knesset member to form a government. That person will be given 28 days to do so, with a potential 14-day extension.
The president has wide discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition. They do not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
On Wednesday morning, Herzog was presented with the official results by Central Elections Committee chairman Justice Noam Sohlberg at a ceremony in Jerusalem.
"In recent days, we have heard voices trying to cast doubt on the election results and to undermine their legitimacy. This is a real danger," Sohlberg said.
"One of the foundations of democracy is the ability to have a peaceful transfer of power. This stems from the understanding that the will of the electorate obligates us all."
Herzog announced that he would begin the consultation process on Wednesday evening.
"In order to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable and good government here for the people of Israel, I expect the factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled," he said.
The president also expressed confidence in the Shin Bet's ability to investigate the allegations of foreign interference in the election and appealed for patience.
But he warned that Arab Israelis - who make up about one fifth of the population and often refer to themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel - "must not be smeared".
"I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently. There is no place for them toward any community in Israel," he said.
Earlier, Sohlberg told a meeting of the Central Elections Committee that the Shin Bet's intelligence appeared to point to a "widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states", some of which were hostile.
It believed further investigation was needed to "connect the dots and determine the scale of the phenomenon with a high degree of certainty", he said.
Last week, Israeli media reported that the committee had been presented with a claim that Qatar had provided funding aimed at increasing voter turnout in Arab communities. Qatar's foreign ministry said it categorically denied the allegation.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the leader of the Jewish Power party and an ally of the prime minister, called on the Shin Bet to arrest all the leaders of Arab parties and interrogate them "until these suspicions are fully clarified".
Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen accused Ben-Gvir and the prime minister of attempting to "steal the election from the public".
On Tuesday, Eisenkot alleged that Netanyahu and his Likud party were "trying to carry out a veritable pogrom against democracy and the rule of law".
His comments came after Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara rejected a reported demand by Shin Bet chief David Zini - an appointee of the prime minister - to interrogate four Arab politicians, saying no evidence of wrongdoing had been presented.
Likud accused Baharav-Miara of trying to "obstruct the investigation and to cover up this serious case of manipulation of the electoral process by foreign actors".

articles.title_orig: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
articles.title_zh: Binance says hackers who stole billions in crypto spent months planning heist
articles.content_orig:
Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.
The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.
Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.
As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."

articles.title_orig: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.title_zh: Data centers lost the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Voters overwhelmingly rejected AI data centers on election night – dealing a major setback to Elon Musk and other tech bigwigs pushing a massive buildout.
At least 50 ballot measures dealing with data centers — either allowing them or limiting them — were up for consideration in states around the country. Voters decided against centers in 47 cases, with the outcome of three votes still pending as of Wednesday afternoon, according to data compiled by Ballotpedia .
The lone favorable outcome for the tech sector occurred in Harwood, ND, where local voters shot down a measure that would have imposed additional review requirements on industrial sites, including data centers, before they can move forward.
The biggest data center rebuke occurred in Ohio, where 21 ballot measures related to controversial sites were up for consideration. Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown focused heavily on the issue in his successful senatorial bid, painting Republican opponent Jon Husted as the “face of data centers.”
The nationwide rejection of data centers coincided with a “blue tsunami” for Democrats, who secured majorities in the House and Senate in a stunning rout.
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa, who defeated longtime incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott, has backed a moratorium on data center projects with an emphasis on making sure the facilities do not strain the power grid.
The outcome of the data center ballot initiatives could give members of the 120th Congress impetus to impose regulation on the sites, according to Ed Mills, a policy analyst for investment firm Raymond James.
“If they consistently see there’s an issue that voters support overwhelmingly, that is going to be their position,” he told the Washington Post.
Top tech executives, such as Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, are expected to come under the microscope with Democrats firmly entrenched in power in Washington.
“Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” Musk, a major Republican donor, wrote on X, referring to one of his pet projects at SpaceX.
Meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Greg Casar, head of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, wrote on X that “AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath.”
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Casar said.

One of Wall Street's biggest AI bulls says the sweeping Democratic victory in the midterm elections will slow the pace of the AI data center build-out in the US over the next two years. AI-related stocks dropped on Wednesday, including Elon Musk-led SpaceX ( SPCX ) and EV maker Tesla ( TSLA ), which fell 4% before trimming losses as the rest of the market surged.
Shares of cloud provider CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and data center-related companies IREN ( IREN ) and Vertiv ( VRT ) also traded lower on Wednesday after Democrats won a majority in the House and Senate on Tuesday night and flipped governorships across key states.
"There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control, especially over the Senate, will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," Yorkville's partner and managing director, Dan Ives, wrote on Wednesday.
Those hurdles, Ives said, will slow the pace of 800 to 1,000 planned AI data centers across the US. The analyst pointed out that the biggest worry for tech investors and the AI trade is the state of Texas, where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from.
Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas Governor race over incumbent Greg Abbott in a surprise result. While Abbott currently has a moratorium on data centers in Texas, the prevailing view was that it would have ended were he reelected.
"Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors," Ives said.
This poses a problem for companies like Texas-based SpaceX, which has been building out its AI infrastructure and taking steps toward a potential merger with Tesla.
"SpaceX and Musk are clearly caught front and center in this spiderweb," said Ives.
"There will be a lot of negotiations and politics on this front especially in Texas which is the foundation of the AI buildout in the US … and Big Tech will need to embrace this new political landscape as of today," he added.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk wrote on X following the election results.
Data center concerns emerged as a key issue in the 2026 midterm elections, with candidates facing growing public opposition to proposed facility locations, the expansion of power infrastructure needed to support them, and concerns that rising electricity demand could drive up consumer costs.
One silver lining for investors may be that political headwinds will force a slowdown in AI capex. AI-related jitters have already weighed on the Tech sector ( XLK ) in recent weeks, with financing concerns hitting neocloud providers that rent out computing capacity, while semiconductor stocks have also retreated.
Long-term, however, Ives remains bullish on the AI trade, as "the Street still is way underestimating the future revenue growth and profitability" stemming from AI.
Fundstrat's Tom Lee is also largely optimistic despite the blue wave.
"President Trump exercises veto power vs any potential 'anti-AI' 'anti-data center' bills," Lee wrote in a note on Tuesday prior to the election results. He also noted that Democrats would likely embrace AI data centers because they bring money and jobs to a community.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s plans new value bundles next year after US traffic falls in third quarter
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's on Wednesday reported mixed quarterly results as traffic to its U.S. restaurants fell, leading to a slight decline in domestic same-store sales.
The fast-food giant reported a 0.2% decrease in sales at its U.S. restaurants that have been open at least 13 months. Even so, the segment performed better than the 0.5% decline that Wall Street anticipated, according to a survey of analysts by StreetAccount.
"In the U.S., we're encouraged by improvement as the quarter progressed following our intervention on value," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said in a statement.
McDonald's same-store sales returned to growth in September after falling in July and August, CFO Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call. However, in response to an analyst question, he clarified that he did not say that U.S. same-store sales would be better in the fourth quarter.
Kempczinski said in August that the company's U.S. business was falling short on execution, particularly on the implementation of its value offerings. Like many restaurants, McDonald's has leaned into discounts to attract budget-conscious diners over the last two years.
To reverse same-store sales declines, McDonald's focused its marketing on its Extra Value Meals and restarted regional and national promotions on its mobile app, which are important to its most frequent diners.
As McDonald's tries to regain its footing in the U.S., the chain is also testing two new value menus, one with mix and match bundles and the other with set combinations of menu items, executives said on the earnings call. The offering that resonates the most with customers and franchisees will be rolled out across the U.S. in early 2027.
Shares of the company closed more than 6% higher Wednesday.
Here's what the company reported compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
The company reported third-quarter net income of $2.49 billion, or $3.51 per share, up from $2.28 billion, or $3.18 per share, a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring charges and other items, McDonald's earned $3.57 per share.
Net revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion.
The company's same-store sales rose 1.5%, lifted by its international segments. That topped analysts' expectations of a 1.3% increase, according to StreetAccount.
McDonald's international developmental licensed markets business, which includes Japan and China, reported same-store sales growth of 4.2%. Wall Street was forecasting same-store sales to rise 2.1% for the division, based on StreetAccount estimates.
The company's international operated division, which includes top markets like Australia and Germany, saw same-store sales growth of 1.4%. Still, the business underperformed Wall Street's expectations. Analysts were projecting same-store sales would rise 2.1%, according to StreetAccount.
"In the majority of our large international markets, we're holding or gaining share," Borden said on the company's conference call. "It's a soft consumer environment, but we're doing well."
France was a weak spot, McDonald's said. Kempczinski said that franchisees in France recently voted on a strategy to turn the business around. In addition to a softer economy in the country, McDonald's has also seen short-term disruptions related to student protests.

articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Bonds Hit New Lows as Texas Data Centers in Crosshairs
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday.
The City of Harwood voted against a charter rule amendment that would have required additional review before city approval of industrial developments, including data centers.
In Ohio, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers," 21 local measures were up for a vote, according to Ballotpedia.
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is also backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
The Ohio Governor's Mansion also turned blue, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the biggest results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, and putting the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
Silicon Valley spent record sums trying to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI, and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , who spent hundreds of millions of dollars this election cycle, largely came up empty.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
The Texas results appear to be a warning sign for the AI industry as a whole.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
—CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

Crude oil inventories in the United States saw a decrease of 900,000 barrels during the week ending October 30, according to new data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) released on Wednesday. The decrease brings commercial stockpiles to 409.8 million barrels, according to government data, which is now 4% below the five-year average for this time of year.
Total commercial petroleum inventories slipped by 8.2 million barrels during the reporting period.
The EIA’s data release follows API’s figures that were released a day earlier, which reported that crude oil inventories had fallen by 5.267 million barrels in the period.
Crude futures were trading down at 10:09 a.m. in New York. Brent futures were trading down at $100.71 per barrel—down $2.89 (-2.79%) on the day and down roughly $15 per barrel from this same time last week. WTI was also trading down on the day, by $2.79 per barrel (-2.90%) on Wednesday morning at $93.30 , down nearly $9 per barrel since this time last week.
For total motor gasoline, the EIA reported that inventories decreased by 200,000 barrels, after growing by 3.9 million barrels in the week prior. The most recent figures showed that average daily gasoline production increased to 9.7 million barrels. For middle distillates, inventories decreased by 3.6 million with production decreasing to an average of 5.2 million barrels daily. Distillate inventories are now 13% below the five-year average.
Total products supplied—a proxy for U.S. oil demand—jumped to a 4 week average of 21.2 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, up 4.2% compared to the same period last year. Gasoline demand averaged 8.6 million barrels per day over the last four weeks, with the distillate four-week average supplied at 4.2 million barrels—up 8.7% year over year.

articles.title_zh: Time to focus on cost of living, says PM after US election results
articles.content_orig:
US tariffs on Canada featured heavily in Michigan and Maine, where Democratic candidates won big on Tuesday
It was the midterm result that many in Canada had hoped for - a Democratic sweep that was in part a repudiation by American voters of Donald Trump's tariff on close trade allies.
"I was doing cartwheels down the street," said Ontario Premier Doug Ford on Wednesday morning, calling it "a victory for Canada".
Tuesday night's result is unlikely to grant Canada relief from those tariffs any time soon, but there is anticipation that the political shifts could create a more favourable environment for Ottawa to get the best deal now that on-again-off-again trade talks are back on.
US voters cited affordability as a main concern heading into the midterms and a survey by the Cato Institute in September , external suggested that about 75% believe the tariffs have raised prices.
In states like Maine and Michigan, tariffs played a significant role in the hard-fought races.
In Maine, incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins clashed with the White House over tariffs.
She successfully lobbied to have some duties that directly affected the state removed, including on road salt, refrigeration equipment and seaweed, but in the end lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.
A similar story played out in Michigan, where state's the automobile manufacturing industry is deeply intertwined with Canada's - and where Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.
Five reasons why Republicans lost so badly
The fight to save Canadian town threatened by Trump's tariffs
In Ohio, Senator-elect Sherrod Brown, who defeated Republican Jon Husted, called the levies a "disaster" and vowed to slash costs for voters by getting rid of them , external .
Democratic leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, now newly empowered, have both pushed to rein in the tariffs on Canada in recent months.
Still, Democratic control of Congress might not do much to move the needle on tariffs. Trump's levies have been largely enacted using executive orders without approval from Congress.
And speaking to Fox News on Tuesday night, Trump touted his "ultimate power" of veto to shut down bills passed by Congress that he does not like.
Some Democratic lawmakers have also supported certain tariffs in the past as a way to protect American manufacturing jobs, and could back keeping some in place.
How the Democratic takeover of the Senate could impact Trump
There are currently several layers of tariffs on Canada, notably on sectors like autos, steel, aluminium and forestry.
After trade talks between Ottawa and Washington collapsed in August, the Trump administration imposed an additional 50% tariff on $20bn (Â£15bn) worth of various Canadian goods, from dairy to cosmetics and furniture.
The US also declared a total import ban on motorcycles, whey protein and alcohol.
Canada retaliated by slapping the US with its own 50% "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs. Most provinces have also banned the sale of US alcohol in retaliation.
Trump had also previously threatened to escalate the trade war with Canada further by â raising tariffs on sectors, including auto manufacturing, as of 1 January.
There were signs that his administration had become more sensitive to the optics of its tariffs on Canada in the run up to the election.
Just a few days before the vote, Trump told reporters that a trade deal is "very close" after speaking with Prime Minister Mark Carney.
Speaking to reporters on Tuesday evening, Carney said of US negotiators that "they're asking less and they're offering more" in recent discussions.
On Wednesday, US-Canada Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the midterm results won't change anything in the short term, and dismissed speculation over  what the new Congress might do when they're seated in the new year as "an interesting discussion at a faculty club luncheon".
"Our approach will not change and we don't intend to speculate on the approach being taken by the Americans," he said.
Pierre Poilievre, leader of Canada's Conservatives, said on Wednesday that "nobody controls Donald Trump".
But he said that midterms results show Canada has "massive leverage" given that the tariffs are broadly unpopular.
"We've got to use that goodwill to pressure for tariff-free trade," he said.
Watch: Key moments from the US midterm election results
Trump may indeed feel more pressure to sign a deal with Canada now that American voters have clearly communicated their frustration, said Colin Robertson, a former Canadian diplomat and a fellow at the Canadian Global Affairs Institute.
"Will this change Trump's mind? It might, because he suffered such a beating at the polls."
But he added it remains to be seen how Trump will react from the bruising midterm loss.
Canada has an ideal window between now and January - when the new Democratic lawmakers are sworn in - to finalise a deal, Robertson noted.
After that, Trump is likely to be distracted by investigations launched by Democrats into Trump's family and finances and some members of his administration, Robertson said.
US trade representative Jamieson Greer also said earlier this year that he had ambitions to have interim deals in place with Canada and Mexico around the North American free trade deal, known as the USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, before the end of the year.
And while Carney struck a more optimistic tone in recent days on the current state of Canada-US trade talks, he also told Politico last month that he was prepared to wait for a new American president if necessary to reach a deal with the US.

articles.title_orig: Secret police files released in Hungary, 37 years after fall of communism
articles.title_zh: Secret police files released in Hungary, 37 years after fall of communism
articles.content_orig:
Hungary released thousands of communist-era secret police records to the public on Wednesday as part of the country's long-delayed effort to come to terms with its repressive past.
The archives, which are now part of a searchable online database, include the names of thousands of former informants who worked for the state security apparatus during four decades of one-party rule.
Although communism ended in Hungary in 1989, attempts to open the files had been repeatedly stalled. Some critics blamed the delay on successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures.
Center-right Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who unseated longtime populist leader Viktor Orban in April, had pledged to grant the public unrestricted access to the records.
"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives on Wednesday.
He said ​some 60,000 ‌names had been made public in the new online database. A second batch of files is expected to be made available by February.
"I ask ‌everyone ​to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity ... as many families will now face difficult information often related to a deceased member of their family," Magyar said. "​It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Hungary was under one-party communist rule from 1949 to 1989.
As was the case in a number of Eastern European countries during the Cold War, secret police in Hungary relied on a vast network of informants to monitor citizens. These informants were often coerced into reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives.
According to estimates from the state security archives, authorities recruited some 150,000 informants, although records for about two-thirds of them no longer exist.
Many files were destroyed in 1956 during Hungary's anti-Soviet uprising, or hidden during the transition to democracy. Some are believed to have been taken to Moscow.
Historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation told the AFP news agency that the move to make the files public was "better late than never."
"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.
He predicted the release would trigger public and private revelations, saying it "could cause some hysteria in the coming months."
Ahead of the publication, rumors had circulated that Former Prime Minister Orban was an informant, but his name did not appear in the digital database on Wednesday.
Orban said on Tuesday that communist secret services had tried to recruit him while he was doing his military service, but he refused.

articles.title_orig: ‘Like opening the Ark Of The Covenant’: Scientists crack code on treasure ship’s padlock — solving 400-year-old maritime mystery
articles.title_zh: ‘Like opening the Ark Of The Covenant’: Scientists crack code on treasure ship’s padlock — solving 400-year-old maritime mystery
articles.content_orig:
As if they found the Davey Jones’ locker combination.
Scientists used cutting-edge scanning techniques to crack the code on a shipwreck’s combination padlock that had been buried in the sand for over 400 years.
“I was blown away that we actually cracked it,” Dr David Williams, a research associate based at Cardiff University’s School of Engineering, told the BBC.
The security device belonged to the Ann Francis , a treasure-loaded vessel that sank off the coast of South Wales in December 1583 after getting caught in a fierce storm while returning from Spain.
The ship’s cargo lay untouched on Morfa Beach in Port Talbot until the late 1990s , when it was discovered by metal detectorist Peter Hughes, who found a massive hoard of gold and silver coins , personal belongings, kitchen utensils, along with the aforementioned brass lock.
While the loot was recovered and donated to the Museum Wales in 2017, Hughes failed to hack the ancient safeguard after years of trying.
“I tried to unlock it for about 20 years, I tried moving the dials, finding the right combinations, and I failed,” the 69-year-old lamented, comparing the caper to the “Da Vinci Code.”
Then, recently, a collaborative team from Museum Wales and Cardiff University finally managed to decipher the gadget’s four-letter password: ANCE.
To get to the bottom of the caper, the shipwreck sleuths relied on micro-computed tomography (CT), a scanning technique normally used to examine the human body, the Independent reported. Williams said he was initially “skeptical” as the tech was “not designed for this particular purpose,” but was nonetheless “open to the challenge.”
Thankfully, by recreating a detailed 3D image of the lock’s internal mechanism, the safecracker was able to see “how the notches lined up with the letters and identify the exact combination.”
This was no mean feat given that the inside featured four rotating rings, each bearing six different letters, yielding a total of 1,296 different combinations (the ancient equivalent of encryption perhaps).
To make things more difficult, there were also letters on the ends that don’t move, suggesting they were decoys used to fool prospective looters.
Dr. Williams said that unveiling the lock of ages’ access code was immensely satisfying, gushing, “It’s not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery.
Meanwhile, the discovery also provided closure for Hughes. “For me, it’s like opening the Ark of the Covenant, and I’m delighted, truly thrilled,” he declared.
It’s yet unclear what the padlock was protecting, but researchers speculate that it could’ve been guarding captain’s chest filled with Spanish silver, high-value textiles, or sensitive maritime documents.
For many experts, the padlock itself was the real buried treasure.
“It was in wonderful condition,” said Museum Wales’ senior curator Siân Iles. “This is a wonderful example of one that still functions as it would have done hundreds of years ago.”
He added, “Because it was found so close to the wreck of the Ann Francis and with all the material that’s part of that collection, it provides a really good context; it allows us to really tightly date it.
The cracked padlock is now on public display at the National Waterfront Museum in Swansea.

articles.title_orig: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.title_zh: French blood storage impacted by freezer hacks as theories swirl about culprits
articles.content_orig:
French authorities say that fridges used in medical facilities to store blood for donations were impacted by recent cyber-attacks by unknown hackers.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said cold rooms storing blood were impacted by hackers, with temperatures set to rise - but staff intervened to protect blood supplies.
"No health impact has been identified and no loss of blood products is to be reported," the EFS said.
Up until now, only supermarkets were known to have been impacted by the hacks.
Meanwhile rumours have been circulating online about Russian hacktivist groups claiming they worked together to hack one of the systems that was used in the attacks which have affected European supermarkets.
Noname057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance posted that they successfully hacked Danfoss which led to speculation that they were the culprits behind the freezer hacks.
But analysts now question whether or not that meant they were behind the supermarket cyber-attacks.
While Russian groups are not being ruled out, experts say Iranian hacktivists or nation state hackers - or even teenagers pulling pranks - could also be the culprits.
Cyber-security researchers at multiple firms are poring over evidence gathered from so-called "honeypots" to provide clues as to who is behind the waves of freezer hacks.
Three separate cyber-security firms have deployed fake freezer software traps to monitor how hackers attempt to use them for attacks.
In cyber-security, a "honeypot" is a digital decoy - such as a fake computer network or file - deliberately set up to look like a vulnerable target to lure and trap hackers.
By monitoring these traps, security experts can safely study an attacker's methods without putting real systems at risk.
According to activity gathered after the first wave of cyber-attacks, the second wave which hit several European countries was highly targeted.
"The fact that all these fridge freezers were hit simultaneously suggests planning and coordination," says Ryan Dewhurst from Spanish cyber-security company Previdian.
The entry point to the affected freezer software products was not difficult to exploit as they were poorly protected, with known attack methods already floating around online.
But experts like Dewhurst say the hacker or hackers had to gather the information about the devices' public IP addresses to create a target list then take time to plan which methods to use and when to execute them.
"Given the reported timing of when the devices had their temperatures increased, which seems to have been overnight for maximum damage - this is further evidence that the attack was planned and co-ordinated," he said.
Another cyber firm which has deployed similar honeypot tech to lure the hackers into revealing their tactics is Strathclyde-based Lupovis.
It had honeypots which appeared to be located around the world, and started seeing activity 10 days before the second wave of cyber-attacks.
Intriguingly, the team saw hackers scanning and probing their fake freezer sites only in Europe.
"We saw none of our honeypots in places like Africa or South America targeted at all," said Lupovis founder Dr Xavier Bellekens.
"Even pots in Ukraine were left alone."
A third company - French cyber-defence firm Sekoia - also noticed scanning activity prior to the second wave of cyber-attacks, but said it could have been automatic scanning without malicious intent.
In a report to its customers, it said evidence suggested the nature of the attack aligned with activity of Russian hacktivists or the Russian government, which is being accused of carrying out so-called "hybrid warfare" cyber-attacks across Europe.
But Sekoia's research also points to Iranian regime hackers or hacktivists too.
"Iranian-aligned actors have an established record of targeting internet-exposed industrial control systems and previous incidents involved the same equipment in Israel and the US - both adversaries of Iran," the report said.
According to Sekoia, about 40 Israeli supermarkets running Danfoss controllers were compromised back in 2022.
Meanwhile in late August, freezers in at least six US military bases were forced into defrost mode, as in France. The controller models remain unconfirmed and investigations are ongoing.
"To date, we have no technical evidence indicating the involvement of Russian-speaking groups," a Sekoia spokesperson told the BBC.
"Furthermore, as NoName057 is not known to effectively conduct operations beyond DDoS attacks and has a history of making false attributions, we remain sceptical of their alleged claim of responsibility."
Distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks work by flooding a website or online service with internet traffic in an attempt to throw it offline, or otherwise make it inaccessible.
Authorities in several countries are actively investigating the hacks and warning supermarkets about potential future attacks.
But no formal attribution has been made.
None of the three cyber firms which have been gathering honey pot data are ruling out that it could be a teenager.
But with the degree of planning necessary the experts all agree it would have to be a well co-ordinated group - and if so, they would expect online bragging to surface soon.
Sekoia also said the possibility remains that all three waves could have been carried out by different and distinct groups or copycats.

Democrats pledge to rein in Big Tech after tapping into voter fears about artificial intelligence.
Democrats’ sweep of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms puts Silicon Valley squarely in the new majority’s sights as they prepare to haul in tech executives for high-profile hearings and set rules for artificial intelligence.
The results mark a sharp rebuke of President Donald Trump’s laissez-faire approach to artificial intelligence and the priorities of some of the industry’s wealthiest figures, including Elon Musk , Marc Andreessen and David Sacks .
Congressional Progressive Caucus Chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) called Tuesday night’s results “the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics.”
Democrats who tapped into voter fears about artificial intelligence and data centers won big Tuesday night, suggesting the tech world is struggling to pitch its AI buildout to the broader public. And the party’s exasperation with the tech industry was on full display Tuesday evening. In his victory speech, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), a potential 2028 presidential contender, lamented “the titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”

articles.title_orig: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.title_zh: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.content_orig:
It was a bad night for data centers . In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has aired ads for months calling his opponent “the face of data centers in Ohio,” cruised to victory to flip a Senate seat. Democrat Chris Pappas, who when seated will be the nation’s first openly gay male senator, mentioned his opposition to data centers in his victory speech and drew massive boos from his crowd in New Hampshire—even though the state has no large-scale data centers under construction.
Elsewhere, two separate Republicans named Derek and Derrick, whose Democratic opponents labeled them “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick,” suffered losses in House races in Ohio and Wisconsin.
As part of last night’s shocking blue tsunami , voters selected candidates with tough policies on data centers at all levels of government, in a clear rebuke to the industry’s buildout in states across the country. Almost a quarter of all voters told NBC News that data centers were “crucial” to their vote, while nearly two-thirds said it was either a major or minor factor.
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Greg Casar, the Texas Democratic congressman, said in a statement .
“Data centers and AI as a technology are fundamentally linked in many voters' minds,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI. “So you can address all of the different concerns with data centers with regards to their energy or their noise, or their pollution, and there would still be significant concerns about what these projects are enabling and the effect is having on opportunities, prices, jobs, society.”
Perhaps some of the biggest shocks for the industry came in the governor’s mansions. In stunning upsets, voters elected Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while putting Cindy Holscher on the cusp of a potential win in Kansas. All of these candidates campaigned not just for increased regulations on the industry, but for data center moratoriums. A pause on data centers in Texas and Georgia especially, two of the biggest hubs for development in the country, could have serious implications for the hundreds of projects planned for each of those states.
“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” says McCoy. “I think we'll likely see the appointment of regulators in various administrative bureaucratic bodies that pose more scrutiny on these projects and an increase in the enforcement of environmental protection regulations.”
Simply being anti-data center wasn’t enough to boost some candidates—especially Republicans. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany, who hit Democrat David Crowley early on in his campaign with ads dubbing him “Data Center David Crowley,” lost his race. (Crowley got more aggressive on the industry as the campaign went on, indicating he would support a pause two weeks before election day.) So did incumbent Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th congressional district, who aired ads slamming his opponent’s past statements that New York “needs” data centers, conceded his race even though the Associated Press has yet to call it.
Throughout the campaign, data centers proved to be a bipartisan topic of concern , and caused fractures within the parties themselves. Earlier this year, WIRED reported how many of Donald Trump’s MAGA loyalists disagreed with the president’s support for AI companies and data centers.
But it’s undeniable that anger about data centers helped elect Democrats. In the weeks leading up to the elections, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee ran ads that highlighted Republicans’ support for data centers or the backing they had received from AI companies.
“Voters aren’t stupid. The data center story is a corruption story. It's an affordability story. It's a Big Tech CEOs influence story,” says Sacha Haworth executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. “That's what voters understood when they cast their ballots and that's why Democrats routed Republicans so, so hard last night, because Republicans could not tell the same story.”
Many of the candidates who won on stricter data center regulations did so despite massive injections of cash from the AI and data center industries to their opponents. In South Carolina, Building the Future, a new industry super PAC, spent $1.5 million to support Darline Graham; she lost last night to Democrat Annie Andrews, who favors a moratorium. (Andrews registered the URL DataCenterDarline.com in late September to hit Graham on her industry connections.) Building the Future also injected more than $1.5 million into the Kansas gubernatorial race to support Republican Ty Masterson against Holscher. And Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence, who made regulations on AI and data centers a cornerstone of his campaign, has declared victory (though without an AP announcement) over Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive races in the country. Barrett had gotten $340,000 from Elon Musk’s America PAC over the course of the race.
“Despite poll after poll making it clear that the conservative rural working-class base was concerned about data centers and the impact of AI, too many politicians in Washington chose big AI’s money over their own base,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, an advocacy group pushing for democratic oversight of AI, said in a statement.
In data center ballot measures across nine states, voters rejected future construction plans, approved moratoriums, and called for greater consultation with and accountability to local communities. Ten states put forth more than 40 questions about data centers on local ballots, according to Ballotpedia, including 21 in Ohio alone. Questions ranged from outright moratoriums to rezoning questions to restrictions on development. Just one county appears to have allowed for more data center development on their ballot, according to Americans for Responsible Innovation president Brad Carson, who was tracking ballot developments throughout the night.
Tech companies appear to be smelling blood in the water. On the day of the midterms, The Hill reported that environmental groups and Big Tech companies were working together as part of a “Responsible Data Center Development Collaborative” to create a framework for data center development. McCoy calls this kind of collaboration the “right next step.”
Meanwhile, as the results rolled in, Musk posted on X , “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title_orig: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures ripped higher on Wednesday, reversing earlier losses, as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections allowed investors to look past the political risk hanging over the market.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 724 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures traded 1% higher, along with Nasdaq-100 futures . Stock futures were down sharply overnight.
Democrats took control of Congress Tuesday night, winning majorities in both the House and Senate. They also scored victories in key gubernatorial races, including Texas.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Wall Street also worried that a clear winner would not emerge Tuesday night. However, those concerns eased after President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.8% in premarket trading, while Tesla shares shed 4.9%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Nebius fell 3.6% and 1%, respectively.
But other parts of the tech trade gained. Microsoft advanced 0.3%, and Amazon climbed 1.1%, as Nvidia moved 0.5% higher. Alphabet was the outlier, trading around 0.4% lower.
U.S. health insurers and hospital operators also advanced, with United Health up 1.4%, Molina Healthcare rising 6.3%, Centene adding 4.7% and HCA Healthcare up 1.44%.
Renewables stocks rallied sharply in premarket trading, while defense stocks fell.
AMD shares popped 6% after the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the result will bring "gridlock" to Washington, but added that the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe", Slimmon said that if the result increases the push for a resolution to the Middle East conflict, that may bring oil prices lower.  "That's been an issue for the Fed, and inflation, and part of the reason that rates are higher."
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.
U.S. renewable energy stocks climbed on expectations of a policy shift. First Solar advanced 8.5%, Bloom Energy gained 5.8%, Plug Power rose 10.6%, Sunrun notched an 8.64% gain, FuelCell Energy was up 6.24% and SolarEdge Technologies moved 4% higher.
Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.
European renewable energy stocks moved sharply higher in early trade as prospects of a decisive Democrat victory in the U.S. midterm elections sparked hopes of a U.S. policy shift on renewables.
Copenhagen-listed Oersted surged 7.3% while Danish peer Vestas advanced 5.2%. The two companies have grappled with uncertainty in their U.S. businesses in recent years, partly as a result of fierce opposition from the Trump administration toward the renewable energy sector.
SMA Solar shares were up 5.5% and Nordex shares added 4.8%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.44% in early trading, as the continent's stocks and major bourses moved higher on the Democrats' clean sweep of the U.S. midterms.
Banks advanced 1.83%, leading gains, with basic resources up 1.71% and utilities rising 0.68%. Food and beverage stocks lost 0.57%, and industrial goods fell 0.37%.
The Italian FTSE MIB was up 0.88%, leading regional bourses. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.22%, while the French CAC 40 rose 0.24% and Germany's DAX gained 0.28%.
Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates amid continued GLP-1 volume growth globally, sending shares up as much as 6% in early trading.
The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.
Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year at constant exchange rates and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
It comes as the Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed Wednesday, as investors assessed a projected Democratic takeover of the U.S. Senate and House, while President Donald Trump appeared to not challenge the results.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.62% to end at 5,683.8, while the small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq added 1.5% to 714.95 in choppy trading.
Japan's Nikkei 225 pared some losses to close 1.42% lower at 62,188.63, and the broad-based Topix declined 0.89% to 3,895.38.
Mainland China's CSI 300 gained 2.31% to 4,101.34, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.43% higher in its last hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.59% to 8,834.5.
— Lee Ying Shan, Lim Hui Jie
The dollar moved lower against most major currencies as the Democrats took control of Congress after the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro was last seen 0.39% higher against the dollar at $1.1235, while the British pound also strengthened against the greenback, rising 0.48% to $1.3476.
The dollar index , which tracks the greenback's strength against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.39% at $101.32.
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower at 4.9311%. The 30-year bond yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.3136%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 1 basis point to 4.6017%.
European stock markets are set to open negative as investors respond to overnight projections of a major Democratic victory in the U.S. midterms.
The Democrats are projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title_zh: Stocks, Bonds Rally After US Vote as Dollar Falls: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 3 basis points lower at 4.9167%. The 30-year bond yield slid 3 basis points to 5.29%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield was broadly flat at 4.6101%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Democrats are on course for a clean sweep, with the party winning at least the House and projected to win the Senate according to a CNBC Election Desk.
The Associated Press is projecting that Democrats have flipped Senate seats from Republicans in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine and Texas.
Stock futures fell sharply as election results rolled in. Contracts tied to the S&P 500 were seen 0.17% lower, and Nasdaq-100 futures slid 0.25%.
AI-related shares, which have led the bull market, paced the overnight decline on fears that Democrats would slow the data center buildout.

articles.title_orig: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.title_zh: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.
